newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish court denies Chinese couple's extradition.
newsitem.headline: Polish court denies Chinese couple's extradition.

text.p: A Warsaw court ruled on Friday that Poland should not extradite two members of China's Mongolian minority, wanted by Beijing for embezzlement, after human rights activists argued that they risked being shot.
The regional court said the couple -- Mandugeqi, 52 and his 42-year-old wife Yinge -- could suffer a violation of their human rights in China if extradited.

Human rights activists and the couple's lawyer had argued that the couple could face the death penalty, often imposed in China for economic crimes, even though Chinese authorities had promised they would not be executed.
"A positive opinion (on extradition) could lead to charges against Poland in the European Court of Human Rights," judge Ewa Gutowska-Sawczuk said in justifying the verdict.
She added that there was no extradition treaty between Poland and China to provide a legal basis for deportation.

The Mandugeqis were detained in Warsaw in August on the basis of an Interpol notice and have since been held in separate jails. Chinese authorities issued an arrest warrant in 1994, the year after the couple left the country.

Their lawyer Wojciech Hermelinski earlier said the pair faced imprecisely-formulated allegations of fraud, failing to repay borrowed money from banks and individuals and of not paying for goods, together involving a total of about 17.5 million yuan ($2.1 million).
The couple argue they repaid practically all they owed and assets they left in China covered any outstanding sums.
The Mandugeqis, who lived in Mongolia before coming to Poland, argue that they had fled China in 1993 as they were wanted because of Mandugeqi's political activities.

An observer at a previous, closed session of the court quoted Mandugeqi as saying he had been jailed in China for eight years on political charges in the 1960s and had since been forced to work for China's security services.
The observer quoted him as saying he had gone to Mongolia in 1993 with thousands of dollars received from the Chinese authorities, and had then failed to return to the country.
The couple's lawyer Wojciech Hermelinski said after the verdict he would ask the Court of Appeals on Monday to order their release. The court will have seven days to decide.
The pair has asked for political asylum in Poland and the application is still being considered.
